alignment.note: Greek and Latin attest a coordinating conjunction (καί / Et) as a separate token, while Syriac fuses the conjunction proclitically into ܘܥܢܐ ('and-answered'); the waw-prefix is a routine Syriac orthographic feature rather than a textual variant.
ἀποκριθείς / ܥܢܐ / respondens — the aorist passive participle of 'answer' is rendered identically across all three; the Syriac verb shares index 0 because the conjunction is fused to the same lexeme.

ὁ Ἰησοῦς / ܝܫܘܥ / Jesus — the Greek definite article before the proper name has no counterpart in Syriac or Latin, both of which lack a definite article in this position; this is an expected typological difference, not a variant.

Greek employs the historic present λέγει ('says'), a vivid narrative tense; Syriac ܘܐܡܪ and Latin ait both render with a past/perfective verb of saying, normalising the tense as is customary in both versions when translating Markan historic presents.

αὐτοῖς / ܠܗܘܢ / illis ('to them') agree as the dative/indirect object; the Vulgate isolates the following colon as a separate token (idx 5) marking the onset of direct discourse, a punctuation feature absent as a discrete token in the Greek (where it is enclitic to αὐτοῖς·).

Greek and Latin use a direct imperative ἔχετε / Habete ('have ye'); Syriac recasts the command periphrastically with ܬܗܘܐ ܒܟܘܢ ('let there be in you'), an existential-possessive construction idiomatic to Syriac for expressing inalienable possession of an abstract quality such as faith.
πίστιν / ܗܝܡܢܘܬܐ / fidem — 'faith' is the shared object across all three witnesses.

θεοῦ / ܕܐܠܗܐ / Dei — the objective/possessive genitive 'of God' is rendered uniformly; the much-debated sense ('faith in God' vs. 'God's faithfulness') is preserved ambiguously in all three traditions without disambiguation.
